claims.text: A pressurized aircraft fuselage repeatedly carries loads caused by the pressure difference between the cabin and the outside air.
An opening interrupts the stress field in a loaded structure, and sharp corners can create localized stress concentrations.
Rounded window edges let structural stress flow more smoothly around an opening and reduce the severe concentrations found at sharp corners.
Investigations of the de Havilland Comet found fatigue and high stress concentrations around squarish window and frame corners, influencing later design and fatigue-testing practice.

script.short: Why are airplane windows rounded instead of square? It is not about the view. It is about how a pressurized cabin carries stress. At altitude, cabin pressure is higher than outside, so the thin fuselage skin is constantly being pushed outward. Cut any window into that skin, and the load has to flow around the opening. A sharp corner forces that load to turn abruptly. Stress bunches into a tiny area instead of spreading smoothly. Repeat that pressure cycle flight after flight, and concentrated stress can help fatigue cracks grow. A rounded corner gives the load a smoother path around the opening, reducing severe stress concentrations. It does not remove stress; it distributes it better. Early de Havilland Comet investigations found high stress concentrations around squarish window frames. Modern rounded windows reflect that hard-earned engineering lesson.
